reasons.C1: Auditable detection of self-funded buyer rings on public payment ledgers is a neglected, operator-relevant problem with a concrete audit path.
reasons.C2: Held-out result is real but wide (0.56 to 1.00), labels share the rule's evidence, independent-feature rule not significant, wallets not shown to be agents.
reasons.C3: Claims and limits are stated plainly, but a 17-page report risks exceeding the 8-page body and withheld tables hamper verification.

levers.C1: Show the flagged wallets are LLM agents and that the rule transfers to a second agent marketplace with independent labels.
levers.C2: Obtain labels from an independent team, evaluate on more held-out families, and run the 21 tests with a published log.
levers.C3: Cut the body to 8 pages with one headline figure and release the 63 withheld case tables in an appendix.

M3.verdict: Most operationally useful idea here, but the evidence chain has label leakage and it is not yet clearly about AI agents.

reasons.C1: Rival coalitions instead of one coalition against a principal is a fresh framing, though coalitions are instructed rather than emergent.
reasons.C2: Pre-registration with hashes and 144 episodes are solid, but no positive control, a post-freeze measure change, p = 0.055, and run files absent.
reasons.C3: Report PDF not seen and no limitations appendix; only README and tables convey the findings.

levers.C1: Show rivalry changes cohesion for emergent, uninstructed coalitions across several model families, with a policy-relevant implication.
levers.C2: Add a positive control, publish raw run files, and confirm the defection effect in a fresh pre-registered replication.
levers.C3: Deliver the 8-page report with a clear headline figure and the Limitations and Dual-Use appendix.

Q5.verdict: Interesting question and careful pre-registration, but the main effect is marginal and the deliverable report is missing.

reasons.C1: Testing whether pricing agents accept an injected cartel offer is a reasonable red-team design with a positive control, but not new.
reasons.C2: No core run: run-log folder empty, replay page holds invented data, only a claimed four-game smoke run; tests do not substitute for results.
reasons.C3: Design is understandable, but the report is a placeholder skeleton and there are no findings to communicate.

levers.C1: Show accepted offers persist into prices across providers and that a defence closes the gap, with a deployable monitoring recommendation.
levers.C2: Run the 60 pre-registered games, pass the positive-control gate, and publish logs with Wilson intervals per condition.
levers.C3: Write the report with results, remove invented demo data, and state clearly what was run versus planned.

T2.verdict: Plenty of scaffolding and tests, but no real experiment ran; invented demo data is a red flag for accountability.

reasons.C1: Replicates a known human cartel study, but testing whether leniency and fines work on LLM sellers is directly policy-relevant and new.
reasons.C2: Positive control, placebo arm, robustness grid shift, call logs and honest 2 of 7 scorecard; one seed per regime and thin reward cells.
reasons.C3: Report body ends on page 8, human-versus-model figure makes the comparison immediate, limitations appendix present.

levers.C1: Add a second provider and derive a concrete enforcement recommendation where LLM and human responses to leniency diverge.
levers.C2: Run multiple seeds per regime, enlarge reward and leniency cartel counts, and expand the positive control beyond three duopolies.
levers.C3: Lead with one sentence on what authorities should change, and put the scorecard table on the first page.

K5.verdict: Most complete controlled experiment in the field, with honest negative replication results and verifiable logs.

reasons.C1: Receiver-side sanitization of vector channels matters for oversight, but channels are non-adaptive, pre-trained before the sprint, and no collusion game.
reasons.C2: Held-out evaluation, reproduce log 10 of 10, text baseline and shuffled-label probe controls; few seeds and no significance tests.
reasons.C3: Figure 1 tells the story at a glance; claims are precise, though the report runs to 13 pages.

levers.C1: Train channels adaptively against snapping and show whether the countermeasure survives inside an actual collusion game.
levers.C2: Add more seeds with significance tests and publish checkpoints so the results can be verified without a request.
levers.C3: Tighten to an 8-page body and state up front which work predates the sprint.

W9.verdict: Rigorous, clean countermeasure result, but off the collusion core and against a non-adaptive adversary.
